title: How JoyoRogo sets your eating target
subtitle: From BMR and activity level to the extra movement your watch or phone picks up. With a worked example and sources.

why.title: BMR and TDEE: what's the difference?
why.p1: BMR is the energy your body uses at complete rest: breathing, keeping your heart beating, staying warm. It's calculated from your weight, height, age and sex using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation (1990).
why.p2: TDEE is the total energy you burn in a day: your BMR, plus everyday movement, plus the energy it takes to digest food. Eat as much as your TDEE and your weight stays the same. JoyoRogo starts from your TDEE, then subtracts a deficit if you want to lose weight, or adds a surplus if you want to gain.
why.p3: We used to start from BMR alone. That turned out too low for almost everyone, because it leaves out daily movement and the energy spent digesting food.

formula.title: TDEE = BMR × factor
formula.p1: TDEE is your BMR multiplied by an activity factor. These are widely used standard numbers, from 1.2 to 1.9, depending on how active your days are. You choose the level.
formula.p2: Digesting and absorbing food also uses energy. This is called the thermic effect of food (TEF), and it's about 5 to 15% of daily expenditure (Westerterp 2004). JoyoRogo uses 10%. Because the factors are based on total expenditure, TEF is already included, so it isn't added again.

levels.title: Five activity levels
levels.intro: Each level has a standard factor. Here's what each one means, some examples, and the TDEE it gives for the person in the worked example below.
levels.tip: Torn between two levels? Pick the lower one, then check whether your weight drops as planned. The app also suggests a level based on your steps and your weight trend (see below).
levels.chart: The higher the level, the bigger the TDEE. The darker part is the BMR, which is the same at every level.
levels.chartLabel: Bar chart of the TDEE for all five levels.

credit.title: Watch and phone data only adds, never subtracts
credit.p1: Your factor already includes an average day's movement, so data from your watch, phone or Health app isn't counted from zero. Only measured movement beyond what your factor already covers is added.
credit.p2: Movement already in the factor = TDEE − BMR − 10% of TDEE (the part for digesting food). For the {{level}} example, that's about {{included}} kcal.
credit.p3: The extra is then multiplied by the percentage you set (default {{pct}}%), and the daily addition is capped (default {{cap}} kcal). The percentage is below 100 because wrist devices aren't accurate at measuring energy: of 7 devices tested, none had an error below 20% (Shcherbina et al. 2017). Workouts you log outside your watch, for example by hand, are added the same way.
credit.chart: Three example days at the {{level}} level. The dashed line marks the movement already in the factor ({{included}} kcal). Only the part above the line is added.
credit.chartLabel: Chart of three days: measured movement of {{a}}, {{b}} and {{c}} kcal against the {{included}} kcal line.
credit.legendBelow: Already in the factor, not added
credit.deskTitle: When your phone stays on the desk
credit.deskBody: A tiny number from a phone you didn't carry no longer reads as a lazy day. If measured movement is below what your factor already covers, nothing is added and your target stays at the base target. Watch or phone data never lowers your target.

recommend.title: Suggestions for a more accurate level
recommend.intro: The level you pick is your best guess. These two checks help confirm it. Both are only suggestions with a Use button, and are never applied automatically.
recommend.stepsBody: If your account has step data on at least 5 of the last 14 days, the average is matched against the Tudor-Locke & Bassett (2004) step index. During onboarding, this suggestion only appears if the data is already there.
recommend.trendBody: Once you've weighed in and logged food regularly for at least 3 weeks (at least 70% of days logged), JoyoRogo works out how much your body actually burns: your average intake, adjusted for your weight change, minus your average logged workouts. That number is divided by your BMR and matched to the nearest level, so you can compare what was measured with what the formula predicts.
recommend.trendNote: The 7,700 kcal per kg rule is only an approximation, because the body adapts as weight changes (Hall et al. 2011). So treat this as a suggestion, not a final answer.

example.title: Worked example
example.intro: A 26-year-old man, 171.5 cm tall, weighing 107.7 kg, aiming for 78 kg by 4 June 2027, calculated on 19 October 2026. BMR = 10 × 107.7 + 6.25 × 171.5 − 5 × 26 + 5 = {{bmr}} kcal. The deficit needed is {{raw}} kcal a day, capped at {{deficit}}.
example.floorNote: At the lowest level, TDEE minus the deficit falls below the minimum intake for men ({{floor}} kcal), so the target is raised to {{floor}} kcal.
example.oldNote: The old method (BMR minus the deficit) gave {{old}} kcal at every level.

cta.title: Try it on your account
cta.body: Go to Profile, then Target & body. Pick your level and see the target for each option.
